title: A Visitor From Another Star Is Made of Dusty Ice
summary:
A comet from another star system is giving scientists a rare glimpse of how planets might form around other stars, thanks to the James Webb Space Telescope.

The comet, called 3I/ATLAS, was discovered entering the solar system in the summer of 2025. It was only the third object found entering the solar system from farther afield in the Milky Way, after 1I/'Oumuamua, seen in 2017, and 2I/Borisov, detected in 2019. Because it offered a rare chance to glimpse the conditions under which such bodies form in other star systems, the telescope was quickly on its trail.

Researchers know 3I/ATLAS was not born in the solar system, but nobody knows around which star it formed. It was likely produced within a planet-forming disk of gas and dust around a young star, possibly 10 to 12 billion years ago, more than twice the age of our solar system, then ejected to wander interstellar space.

When the telescope viewed 3I/ATLAS three times between August 2025 and April 2026, scientists found a puzzle: in our solar system's comets, water-ice creates a strong line at three microns plus weaker lines at 1.5 and two microns, but for 3I/ATLAS the shorter lines were missing while the three-micron line remained strong.

"That combination was a puzzle," said research lead author Silvia Protopapa of the Southwest Research Institute. "The strong three-micron band points to water-ice in the coma, but the weak or absent shorter-wavelength bands suggest the ice is not in the form we usually see in solar system comets."

Modeling suggested 3I/ATLAS was composed of sub-micron grains of dirty water-ice, rich in dust, unlike our solar system's much cleaner, almost pure water-ice grains. "Those grains hold clues to the conditions where the comet was born," Protopapa said.
why_it_matters: An interstellar comet is a sample from another star system, so its makeup can show whether planets elsewhere formed like ours or in very different conditions.

background_read: A comet is a chunk of ice and dust left over from when a star system formed, and it can grow a glowing tail as it nears a star.
Most comets we see were born in our own solar system, but a few come from other star systems and pass through ours.
Scientists study the light from a comet to learn what its ice and dust are made of, which can hint at where it was born.
Planet-forming disks are rings of gas and dust around young stars where new planets may slowly take shape.
